playbook:
I pledge [pledge: y] whenever the table is pledging Y; I treat the pledge as a tool to keep the all-Y +1 line alive, not as a promise I must keep.

Until the multiplier rounds, I default to [pick: y]; shared +1s build a base and let me see whether anyone defects.

If everyone else has shown repeated Y and I want a lead on a low-multiplier round, I take exactly one solo [pick: x] for +3 while the others eat −1; I do not keep pressing X after that unless the endgame calls for it.

After I play X, I watch for copycats; once anyone else starts choosing X, I immediately go back to Y, because 4X is the disaster outcome and even 2–3 X is worse than safe cooperation.

I never choose X hoping for a “fair” split; I choose X only when I expect to be alone or nearly alone with it.

On high-multiplier rounds I become more willing to defect: if the opponents are still locked into Y, I pick [pick: x], there or especially later; the bigger the multiplier, the more a solo X dominates.

On the final x10 round, if everyone else has pledged Y and their recent history is all Y, I break any pledge and play [pick: x]; that is the highest-value exploitation point and there is no future reputation to protect.

If I am behind late, I prefer X over passive Y; if I am ahead but opponents look unstable or spiteful, I only use X when a credible all-Y profile makes me the lone X.

I do not waste the early table talk trying to bluff X; I say Y, let others settle, and reserve my real aggression for the round that multiplies it.
